screens.title: Reentrancy & Integer Overflows: Critical Smart Contract Risks
screens.subtitle: Why external calls and unchecked arithmetic break assumptions and how to defend your contracts

narration.text: Smart contracts manage real value in a transparent, adversarial environment. In this lesson we focus on two classes of mistakes that have caused major losses: reentrancy, where an external call can reenter your contract before state is updated, and integer overflows and underflows, where arithmetic wraps and corrupts balances. You will see a classic vulnerable Ether store, a reentrancy attack pattern inspired by the DAO incident, and practical fixes: the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern and mutex-style reentrancy guards. We will also examine counter examples that show why older Solidity versions needed SafeMath and how Solidity 0.8.0 and later change arithmetic behavior. Throughout, you’ll practice writing tests that first demonstrate an exploit and then verify the patched contract resists it. By the end you should be able to spot ordering mistakes, pick the appropriate defensive pattern, and design tests that intentionally trigger overflow or reentrancy to prove safety. Think about why a simple external transfer can change assumptions about control flow; that question will guide our first example.

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Detect and defend against reentrancy and integer over/underflow with CEI, reentrancy guards, SafeMath or Solidity 0.8+ arithmetic, and targeted tests.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify reentrancy in code, explain how the DAO-style attack works, and implement the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern as a primary defense. You will recognize where state updates must occur and how external calls change control flow. You will also identify integer overflow and underflow risks in older Solidity versions and know when to use SafeMath or upgrade to Solidity 0.8.0+. Each objective is paired with a small practice: build a failing exploit test, then patch the contract and prove the fix with a passing test. That test-first approach helps you not only fix code, but verify the fix under adversarial conditions. These skills matter because smart contracts are immutable once deployed; testing and patterns you learn here reduce the chance of costly errors. As you work, ask whether an external transfer could let a caller change contract state or whether arithmetic ops could wrap unexpectedly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Patterns
screens.subtitle: Skills and test habits to verify security fixes

narration.text: Security is not only patterns but also repeatable practice. This section emphasizes writing unit tests designed to exploit a vulnerability, then proving the patch prevents it. You will learn to craft attacker scenarios that call withdraw with unexpected inputs, deploy malicious fallback contracts, and assert behavior before and after a fix. We will also highlight two defensive tools you should master: the reentrancy guard, which works like a mutex to block nested calls, and SafeMath for arithmetic in older Solidity. Finally, you will practice reading code for the exact ordering of checks, effects, and interactions so you can argue why a change is safe. These habits—test-first exploit construction, clear CEI ordering, and deliberate use of built-in or library arithmetic checks—are what convert a secure idea into a verifiable, auditable contract. Keep these objectives in mind as we walk code examples and tests that illustrate both the attack and the fix.

screens.title: What is Reentrancy?
screens.subtitle: Definition, why it breaks assumptions, and a simple thought experiment

narration.text: Reentrancy is a control-flow vulnerability that occurs when a contract makes an external call to untrusted code and that external code calls back into the original contract before the previous execution completes. The problem is an assumption violation: functions often assume state variables remain stable across an external call, but if that call yields control to attacker code, state may still be unchanged and exploitable. Imagine a withdraw function that reads a user balance, sends funds, and then zeros the balance. If a malicious fallback calls withdraw again while the balance is still nonzero, the attacker can extract funds repeatedly. A concrete example is an Ether store that calls back to msg. sender before setting balances[msg. sender] = 0. A common misconception is that transfers are always safe; while transfer and send impose a small gas stipend, they do not eliminate reentrancy in every scenario. The safe mental model is to assume any external call can reenter. The key defensive claim is simple: do checks, then effects, then interactions, or add a mutex. As a takeaway, always ask: can control flow return to this contract before state changes are final?

keyIdea.title: Reentrancy defined
keyIdea.text: An external call allows attacker code to reenter before your state update completes; assume any external call can reenter and defend accordingly.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › What is Reentrancy?
Definition

Reentrancy explained

A call to untrusted code can return control to your contract before state changes finish, violating assumptions and enabling repeated actions.

Thought experiment: withdraw reads balance, sends funds, then sets balance to zero — a fallback can call withdraw again.
Misconception: using transfer() always prevents reentrancy. Not guaranteed; assume reentry is possible and design accordingly.
Key Takeaway

Treat every external call as potentially reentrant. Order state updates before interactions or add a reentrancy guard.

Analogy & Example
Analogy: Imagine unlocking a vault, passing the key to an untrusted courier, and then updating the inventory only after the courier has left. If the courier returns before inventory is updated, they can take more items.
Concrete example: the vulnerable EtherStore withdraw pattern shows external call before balances[msg.sender] = 0 allowing repeated withdrawals.
Check your understanding: ask whether any external call in your function can cause state-dependent logic to run again before the state is updated.

screens.title: Vulnerable EtherStore: Code Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Read the withdraw flow and spot the vulnerable ordering

narration.text: Let's walk through the EtherStore vulnerable withdraw function line by line. The contract stores balances per address. When a user calls withdraw, the function reads the stored amount and requires a positive balance. The vulnerable step is that the contract then performs an external call to the user address to transfer Ether before it sets the stored balance to zero. That call allows an attacker’s fallback to execute and call withdraw again, because the balance has not yet been updated. A correct mental model is to mark the state update as atomic and final before handing control to external code. In the vulnerable example, the order is read balance, external call, then set balance to zero — this ordering is the direct cause of repeated withdrawals. When you read a withdraw or transfer function in reviews, scan for any pattern that does external transfer before state mutation. A good test is to deploy an attacker contract with a fallback that calls withdraw again and confirm the victim’s balance reduces multiple times. This concrete audit habit helps you find reentrancy without needing formal tools.

keyIdea.title: Vulnerability hotspot
keyIdea.text: External calls that occur before state updates are the primary reentrancy risk; always audit withdraw-like functions for ordering mistakes.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Vulnerable EtherStore
Code
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract VulnerableEtherStore {
    mapping(address => uint256) public balances;

    function deposit() public payable {
        balances[msg.sender] += msg.value;
    }

    function withdraw() public {
        uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
        require(amount > 0, "No funds to withdraw");

        // Vulnerable point: external call before state update
        (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}("");
        require(success, "Transfer failed");

        balances[msg.sender] = 0; // State update happens after external call
    }

    function getBalance() public view returns (uint256) {
        return address(this).balance;
    }
}
Explainer
  • Read amount from storage and check it is positive.
  • External call to msg.sender happens before writing balances[msg.sender] = 0.
  • An attacker can reenter during that external call and withdraw repeatedly.
Common-mistake: assuming external transfers are safe because they look simple. Control can switch to attacker code.
Pro-tip: unit test with an attacker fallback that calls withdraw again to confirm vulnerability.
Key Takeaway

If your function calls external code and then changes important state, the function is a reentrancy risk.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) Pattern
screens.subtitle: A simple ordering rule to prevent reentrancy

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prescribes three ordered steps to make external calls safe. First, perform all checks: validate inputs, require sufficient balances, and assert preconditions. Second, apply all effects: mutate contract state to record the operation’s outcome. Third, perform interactions: make external calls, transfers, or call other contracts. This ordering ensures that when control leaves the contract, the internal state already reflects the operation, so a reentrant call cannot repeat the same action. A concrete transformation of the vulnerable withdraw replaces the sequence by setting balances[msg. sender] = 0 before the call. A misconception to avoid is thinking CEI alone always solves every problem; certain complex flows still benefit from a reentrancy guard because multiple state variables or external dependencies add complexity. The practical rule is: adopt CEI as first defense, add a ReentrancyGuard when functions remain complex, and always write tests that simulate an attacker calling back in. That test-driven approach confirms CEI works for your specific contract shape. Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) Pattern means checks, then effects, then interactions — order state updates before external calls so reentrant callbacks cannot repeat past actions.. In practical terms, a simple ordering rule to prevent reentrancy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: CEI rule
keyIdea.text: Checks, then Effects, then Interactions — order state updates before external calls so reentrant callbacks cannot repeat past actions.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Checks-Effects-Interactions
Pattern

Checks → Effects → Interactions

Checks

Validate balances, permissions and return early on failure.

Effects

Update storage to reflect the operation before any external call.

Interactions

Call external contracts or transfer funds after state is final.

Key Takeaway

Order matters. CEI reduces reentrancy windows and makes reasoning about state easier during audits.

Example Transformation
// Effect before interaction
uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
require(amount > 0);
balances[msg.sender] = 0; // Effect
(bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}(""); // Interaction
require(success);
Misconception: CEI is sufficient for all cases. In multi-step functions or when calling third-party contracts that depend on multiple state variables, add a mutex to be safe.

screens.title: ReentrancyGuard: Mutex-style Defense
screens.subtitle: How a simple guard prevents nested calls

narration.text: A reentrancy guard implements a mutex: it marks a function as entered and disallows reentry while it runs. The common pattern uses a status variable set when entering and cleared when leaving. If a reentrant call is attempted, the status check fails and the call reverts. This is useful when CEI is difficult to apply across many state variables or when multiple interactions must happen together. A practical example is OpenZeppelin’s ReentrancyGuard which sets a private status and provides a nonReentrant modifier. A misconception is that a guard replaces correct ordering—guards and CEI are complementary. Use CEI to reduce the risk surface and a guard to catch unexpected reentry during complex operations. When testing a guard, deploy a malicious fallback that attempts to call back into the guarded function; you should observe a revert. As a design decision, guards simplify reasoning for auditors because they make nested calls impossible, but remember to clear the status even on revert paths and avoid patterns that could lock the contract forever. ReentrancyGuard: Mutex-style Defense means a reentrancy guard prevents nested calls by blocking entry when the function has already been entered; use it together with cei for robust defense.. In practical terms, how a simple guard prevents nested calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Mutex defense
keyIdea.text: A reentrancy guard prevents nested calls by blocking entry when the function has already been entered; use it together with CEI for robust defense.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › ReentrancyGuard
Pattern

Mutex-style guard

enter(): require(status != ENTERED); status = ENTERED; ... status = NOT_ENTERED;
When a reentrant call occurs, the require check fails and the call reverts. This reduces the risk when multiple state updates and external calls are necessary within one function.
When to use
  • CEI is best first choice; add guard for complex flows
  • Guards are audit-friendly and explicit about reentry policy
  • Test with attacker fallback contracts to confirm blocking
Common mistake

Forgetting to reset the guard status on all exit paths can lock functions; ensure status changes run in a finally-like pattern or rely on modifiers that handle resets.

screens.title: Integer Overflow and Underflow
screens.subtitle: What wrapping means and why attackers exploit it

narration.text: Integer overflow happens when an arithmetic operation yields a value greater than the type can represent, and the result wraps around to a low value. Underflow is the opposite: subtracting below zero wraps to a very large number. For example, using an eight-bit unsigned integer, starting at 255 and adding one yields zero; starting at zero and subtracting one yields 255. Attackers can use wrapping to bypass checks or inflate balances. A vulnerable counter that increments and decrements a uint8 demonstrates this clearly: if decrement on zero underflows, the counter becomes 255. A major practical point is that Solidity behavior depends on compiler version: Solidity 0.8.0 and later revert automatically on overflow or underflow, removing the wrap and causing a revert. Before 0.8.0, libraries like OpenZeppelin’s SafeMath provided checked arithmetic that reverted on unsafe operations. A common misconception is that checks like require(balance >= amount) are enough; while necessary, they are not a substitute for arithmetic safety in older compilers. Always test boundary values to catch wrapping behavior in your version of Solidity. Integer Overflow and Underflow means overflows and underflows wrap integer values in older solidity; use safemath or upgrade to 0.8.0+ to make operations revert on unsafe arithmetic.. In practical terms, what wrapping means and why attackers exploit it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Wrapping arithmetic
keyIdea.text: Overflows and underflows wrap integer values in older Solidity; use SafeMath or upgrade to 0.8.0+ to make operations revert on unsafe arithmetic.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Overflow & Underflow
Definition

Overflow and underflow

Example: uint8 x = 255; x++; // wraps to 0 in older Solidity
Example: uint8 x = 0; x--; // wraps to 255 in older Solidity
Attackers exploit wrapping to bypass checks or to inflate balances. Always test boundary arithmetic and choose the correct protections for your compiler version.
Defenses
  • Solidity 0.8.0+: arithmetic reverts on overflow/underflow
  • Solidity < 0.8.0: use SafeMath for checked operations
  • Write boundary tests that add to max or subtract from zero
Common mistake

Assuming modern compiler behavior when your project uses an older pragma can leave you exposed; confirm the pragma and test boundaries.

screens.title: VulnerableCounter: Underflow Demonstration
screens.subtitle: How a small uint type wraps and how to patch it

narration.text: The VulnerableCounter example uses an explicit small integer type to make wrapping obvious: uint8 count starts at zero. The increment and decrement functions demonstrate wrap behavior: increment at max wraps to zero, decrement at zero wraps to max. In Solidity versions before 0.8.0 a decrement below zero would not revert and would instead wrap to 255, enabling logic that depends on count to break or be exploited. A concrete exploit test calls decrement when the counter is zero and then asserts the counter has become a very large number. The patch options are twofold: switch the pragma to ^0.8.0 so arithmetic checks revert on unsafe operations, or keep the older pragma and import OpenZeppelin’s SafeMath for checked arithmetic. SafeMath’s sub function reverts on underflow. When patching, update increment and decrement to use safe add and sub, and then rerun the exploit test expecting a revert. Keep in mind that choosing a larger integer type does not eliminate logic errors; boundary testing is the correct habit. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Underflow demo
keyIdea.text: Using a small uint shows wrapping clearly; fix by using SafeMath in older compilers or upgrading to Solidity 0.8.0+ which reverts on wrap.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › VulnerableCounter
Vulnerable code (Solidity < 0.8.0)
pragma solidity ^0.7.0;

contract VulnerableCounter {
    uint8 public count = 0;

    function increment() public {
        count++; // overflow if count == 255
    }

    function decrement() public {
        count--; // underflow if count == 0
    }
}
Patch options
Option A: Upgrade pragma to ^0.8.0 so arithmetic reverts on wrap. Option B: Use SafeMath and call add/sub functions that revert on unsafe arithmetic.
After patch: write tests that attempt the same out-of-range operation and expect a revert.
Note: switching to a larger integer type only postpones the wrap; explicit checks or SafeMath are the correct fix for logic safety.
Check your understanding

Write a test that increments to 255 and then increments once more. Observe whether the counter wraps or reverts depending on your Solidity version or SafeMath usage.

screens.title: Exploit and Patch: Wallet Underflow Lab
screens.subtitle: A guided test-first exercise for underflow and the patch workflow

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through exploiting and patching an underflow in a simple Wallet contract that intentionally uses pragma ^0.7.0. Start by deploying the vulnerable contract and seeding balances. Create an attacker script that calls withdraw with an amount larger than the target balance. The exploit test should show the target address’s stored balance wrapping to a large number. Next, modify the contract to use SafeMath or switch the pragma to ^0.8.0 and redeploy. Rerun the same test and assert that the transaction now reverts. When writing tests, include explicit balance checks before and after, and assert specific revert messages where possible. A useful misconception check: some developers add only a require(balance >= amount) but forget to use SafeMath; if an attacker can manipulate balance between check and subtraction, the underflow may still happen. The practice of writing an exploit test first forces you to see the exact failure mode and then prove the fix with a passing test. That verification habit is the core outcome of this lab. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Underflow Lab
Test Template
// Test 1: Exploit
// 1. Deploy VulnerableWallet (pragma ^0.7.0)
// 2. Deposit balances for owner and attacker
// 3. Attacker calls withdraw(amount > balance)
// 4. Assert attacker wallet balance in contract becomes very large (underflow)

// Test 2: Patch

// 2. Deploy patched contract

// 4. Expect revert
Practical tips
  • Seed attacker with a small deposit so withdraw is plausible
  • Use precise asserts: expect(balance).to.be.gt(initial) for underflow exploit
  • After patch, expect transaction to revert or the balance to remain unchanged
Key Takeaway

Testing the exploit before the fix makes the vulnerability obvious and gives you a regression test to prevent reintroduction.

screens.title: SafeMath vs. Solidity 0.8.0+
screens.subtitle: Two approaches to arithmetic safety and when to use each

narration.text: There are two practical approaches to prevent arithmetic wrapping in Solidity projects. For codebases using Solidity versions older than 0.8.0, SafeMath provides explicit checked operations that revert on overflow or underflow. The pattern is to replace raw arithmetic with SafeMath’s add, sub, mul, and div functions to ensure operations fail rather than wrap. For codebases on Solidity 0.8.0 and later, the compiler inserts automatic checks that revert on unsafe arithmetic, reducing the need for an external library. The trade-offs are straightforward: SafeMath adds explicit function calls and clarity for older code, while upgrading the compiler simplifies code but requires confirming other behaviors and compatibility. A common misconception is that upgrading the compiler is always the cheap fix; in mature projects, dependency constraints or legacy bytecode compatibility may make using SafeMath more practical. In all scenarios you should write boundary tests that attempt max and zero values. The correct engineering choice depends on your project’s constraints, but the testing discipline remains the same. SafeMath vs. Solidity 0.8.0+ means use safemath for solidity <0.8.0; rely on compiler-checked arithmetic for 0.8.0+. always verify with boundary tests.. In practical terms, two approaches to arithmetic safety and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Two defenses
keyIdea.text: Use SafeMath for Solidity <0.8.0; rely on compiler-checked arithmetic for 0.8.0+. Always verify with boundary tests.

content.html:
Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › SafeMath vs Compiler Checks
SafeMath (pre-0.8.0)
Use SafeMath library

Replace x = x.add(1) and x = x.sub(1) to ensure operations revert on wrap.

Useful when project cannot upgrade compiler due to dependencies. Adds explicit safety at the call site.
Solidity 0.8.0+
Built-in checked arithmetic

Arithmetic operations revert automatically on overflow or underflow, simplifying code and reducing library use.

When upgrading, validate existing contracts and tests, and still include boundary tests to document behavior for auditors.

screens.title: Writing Tests for Exploits and Fixes
screens.subtitle: Test structure, assertions, and attacker scaffolding

narration.text: Effective security testing begins with a failing test that reproduces the exploit and concludes with a passing test that verifies the patch. For reentrancy, the test structure deploys the vulnerable contract, deploys an attacker contract with a fallback that calls back to withdraw, funds attacker and victim, runs the attack, and asserts the victim contract balance reaches zero or the attacker’s internal balance inflates. For underflow, the test attempts arithmetic out-of-bounds operations and asserts wrapping behavior in older compilers or a revert in patched contracts. Use precise assertions: for example, expect(finalAttackerBalance). to. be. gt(initial) for an underflow test or expect(transaction). to. be. revertedWith(...) after patching. Also include gas and revert checks for transfer/call variants to ensure your assumptions about gas stipends are validated. A common pitfall is asserting only high-level outcomes without checking intermediate invariants; include checks for storage variables before and after the exploit. These tests become your regression suite that prevents accidental reintroduction of vulnerabilities. Writing Tests for Exploits and Fixes means write exploit tests that fail, then patch and re-run tests to prove the vulnerability is fixed. check intermediate invariants and final balances.. In practical terms, test structure, assertions, and attacker scaffolding. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Write exploit tests that fail, then patch and re-run tests to prove the vulnerability is fixed. Check intermediate invariants and final balances.

screens.title: Common Mistakes & Review Checklist
screens.subtitle: A short audit checklist to prevent regressions

narration.text: Before shipping a contract, run a short checklist focused on the vulnerabilities we covered. First, scan all functions that make external calls and verify CEI ordering: perform require checks, update state, then interact. Second, look for withdraw or transfer patterns that call msg. sender or other contracts — those are high risk. Third, confirm your Solidity pragma: if it's older than 0.8.0, ensure SafeMath is applied to all arithmetic or consider upgrading and running full test suites. Fourth, use a reentrancy guard when a function must perform multiple state changes and external calls together. Fifth, add targeted unit tests that attempt exploits and assert either successful mitigation or revert messages. A common mistake is assuming transfer() is fully safe; while it limits gas, it is not a semantic defense. Another mistake is relying on larger types instead of explicit checks. The final step is to include these tests in your CI so regressions are caught automatically. This checklist turns lessons into reproducible engineering practice. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part A
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to keep front of mind

narration.text: These three concepts are the foundation for securing withdraw-like functions and arithmetic operations. First, reentrancy describes when an external call returns control to your contract before its state is updated, enabling repeated execution. Second, the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern prescribes performing checks, then updating state, and only afterwards making external calls; this ordering greatly reduces reentrancy windows. Third, a Reentrancy Guard acts as a mutex to explicitly block nested calls when CEI is insufficient. Remember to pair patterns and guards with tests that reproduce and then block attacks. These three ideas together form an auditable, testable defense strategy for functions that transfer funds or call external contracts. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts
Reentrancy

An external call can reenter your contract and repeat operations if state is not updated first.

Checks-Effects-Interactions

Perform checks, then update state, and finally make external interactions to minimize reentrancy windows.

Reentrancy Guard

A mutex-like guard blocks nested calls and makes reentry explicit and auditable.

Summary

Combine ordering, guards, and tests to form a provable defense against nested-call attacks.

screens.subtitle: Three more ideas to secure arithmetic and testing

narration.text: These three concepts help you prevent arithmetic exploits and ensure fixes are real. First, integer overflow and underflow cause wrap-around behavior in older Solidity versions and can be exploited to manipulate balances. Second, SafeMath provides checked arithmetic helpers for Solidity versions below 0.8.0 and should be applied consistently when upgrading is not feasible. Third, write targeted tests that first reproduce the exploit and then confirm the patched contract reverts on the same inputs. Together these provide arithmetic safety and verification. Always test boundary values and include these tests in your CI pipeline so regressions are caught before deployment. Key Concepts — Part B means prevent wrapping with safemath or compiler checks and make tests the final proof that a vulnerability is fixed.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 06 › Chapter 6.5 › Key Concepts
Integer Overflow

Operations exceeding max values wrap in older compilers and can be exploited.

SafeMath

A library for checked arithmetic on projects using older Solidity versions.

Exploit Tests

Write tests that reproduce the exploit and verify the patched contract reverts or prevents it.

Final takeaway

Combine defensive code patterns with reproducible tests. That combination is the strongest practical guarantee against reentrancy and arithmetic exploits.
